details:
**A Modest Proposal**
Swift's 1729 satirical pamphlet that "proposes" solving Irish poverty and famine by having poor Irish parents sell their one-year-old children as food for the rich. It is the most common giveaway for Swift and mocks the heartless economic thinking of English landlords and policymakers.

**"A young healthy child... is, at a year old, a most delicious, nourishing, and wholesome food"**
The deadpan central claim of A Modest Proposal. The narrator suggests children can be stewed, roasted, baked, or boiled, or served in "a fricassee, or a ragout," and calculates that 120,000 children could be sold each year.

**Gulliver's Travels**
Swift's 1726 satirical novel in four voyages, narrated by the ship's surgeon Lemuel Gulliver. He visits Lilliput, Brobdingnag, Laputa (along with Balnibarbi, Glubbdubdrib, Luggnagg, and Japan), and finally the land of the Houyhnhnms. Gulliver first sails as a surgeon on the Antelope, and his second voyage is on the Adventure.

**Lilliput and Blefuscu**
The first voyage of Gulliver's Travels. Gulliver is shipwrecked and wakes up tied to the beach by the six-inch-tall Lilliputians. Lilliput is at war with the neighboring island of Blefuscu, and Gulliver helps by wading across and stealing the Blefuscudian fleet, though he later flees to Blefuscu.

**Big-Endians and Little-Endians**
The factions in Gulliver's Travels whose conflict centers on whether a boiled egg should be broken at the big end or the little end. The pointless dispute satirizes the religious conflicts between Catholics and Protestants in Europe.

**Houyhnhnms and Yahoos**
The final voyage of Gulliver's Travels takes him to a land ruled by the Houyhnhnms, rational talking horses, who keep the filthy, brutish, human-like Yahoos as domesticated animals. Gulliver comes to believe the Houyhnhnms are more civilized than humans and is reluctant to return to human society.

**A Tale of a Tub (Peter, Martin, and Jack)**
Swift's first major work (1704), a religious satire in which a father leaves coats to his three sons with a will forbidding any changes. Peter represents the Roman Catholic Church, Martin represents Lutherans and Anglicans (after Martin Luther), and Jack represents Calvinists and Dissenters (after John Calvin). The work was attacked by William Wotton.

**"Shoulder-knots" and the "Digression on Madness"**
Episodes in A Tale of a Tub. The brothers, wanting to follow fashion, justify adding shoulder-knots to their coats by picking the individual letters of the word out of their father's will. The book also includes digressions, such as the "Digression Concerning Madness," and describes the Aeolists, who believe wind is the essence of all things.

**The Battle of the Books (the spider and the bee)**
A satire published with A Tale of a Tub depicting a battle between ancient and modern authors in St. James's Library, part of the "Ancients versus Moderns" debate. It contains an allegory in which a self-spinning spider represents the Moderns and a bee gathering from nature represents the Ancients, and it ends with an episode about the modern scholars Bentley and Wotton.

**Psalmanazar the Formosan**
A Modest Proposal cites George Psalmanazar, a famous impostor who claimed to be a native of Formosa (Taiwan). Swift's narrator reports Psalmanazar's tale that in Formosa the bodies of executed young people were sold as delicacies, including a girl crucified for trying to poison the Emperor.

**"Lessen the number of Papists"**
One of the "advantages" listed in A Modest Proposal: since Catholics have the most children, eating Irish babies would reduce the number of "Papists," whom the narrator calls the nation's "most dangerous enemies." Other advantages include making the children's skin into "admirable gloves for ladies, and summer boots for fine gentlemen."

**Isaac Bickerstaff and John Partridge**
Under the pseudonym Isaac Bickerstaff, Swift mocked the astrologer and almanac-maker John Partridge in 1708 by "predicting" his death and then publishing an account of that death, insisting Partridge was dead despite his protests.

**Laputa (the flying island and the flappers)**
The third voyage of Gulliver's Travels includes Laputa, a flying island of absent-minded intellectuals so lost in thought that servants called "flappers" must strike their ears and mouths with bladders to get their attention. Their houses are badly built, with no right angles, because of their impractical geometry.

**Brobdingnag**
The second voyage of Gulliver's Travels, a land of giants in which Gulliver is tiny. The King of Brobdingnag, after hearing Gulliver describe England, calls humans "the most pernicious race of little odious vermin."

**Stella (Esther Johnson) and Journal to Stella**
While Swift served as secretary to Sir William Temple, he tutored the young Esther Johnson, whom he called "Stella." He wrote her the letters collected as Journal to Stella and many poems, and it is rumored they were secretly married. He was also Dean of St. Patrick's Cathedral in Dublin.

**The Drapier's Letters**
Writing as "M. B. Drapier," Swift published pamphlets in the 1720s protesting William Wood's patent to mint copper coins ("Wood's halfpence") for Ireland, a campaign that made him an Irish patriotic hero.

**Other poems and essays ("The Lady's Dressing Room," "A Meditation upon a Broomstick")**
In "The Lady's Dressing Room," the speaker sneaks into Celia's dressing room and is disgusted by the filth he finds, concluding that "such gaudy tulips raised from dung." "A Meditation upon a Broomstick" calls man a "topsy-turvy creature," and "An Argument Against Abolishing Christianity" ironically defends nominal Christianity. Swift also wrote "we have just enough religion to make us hate, but not enough to make us love one another" and that a true genius is known because "the dunces are all in confederacy against him."
